# Global cap covers and preserving zero-fiber extension

This note separates a globally valid cap cover from the geometric existence of a zero-fiber birth. Global coverage alone does not force any preserving extension. The obstruction below has a nonempty depth region and a full-dimensional globally mixed-lattice-free auxiliary polytope, so it does not rely on the weaker finite-original-base certificate. It lies above the OC threshold and is not a variational minimum.

## 1. The globally covering certificate can also be obtained in the empty-region case

Section1 of `candidate d2b290ebd8e35052` constructs a bounded full-dimensional polytope Q avoiding the entire mixed lattice, with nonvertical outward caps of mass<T. This construction does not assume the exact depth region is nonempty. Section2 supplies finitely many projection-facet inequalities, each arising from a positive continuous-normal circuit of size<=d+1.

Apply Doignon directly to those projection-facet halfspaces. A subfamily of at most2^n already has intersection disjoint from Z^n. For each integer base z, at least one retained inequality is strictly violated. In that group the positive weighted sum of cap margins is positive and independent of the continuous coordinate. Therefore at least one constituent OPEN cap contains every given point over z. The retained groups cover ALL integer fiber planes, including bases outside the original projection.

This route loses the extra guarantee in the finite-P expansion that its integer facet witnesses belong to the original P. It preserves the actual real circuit contacts and all original strict cap-mass bounds. Thus one need not infer global coverage from finite-P witnesses.

I checked the auxiliary-Q empty-case construction as follows. After a generic small perturbation, every n+d normals are independent and the full list positively spans the ambient space. The maximum of the corresponding affine margins is coercive; its minimum is positive when the intersection is empty. At the first common threshold expansion making the intersection nonempty, the active normals have a positive dependence. Its minimal support has exactly n+d+1 members, by generic independence. Their weighted slacks vanish at every feasible point, so all are equalities, determining a unique point. A sufficiently small translation moves its integer projection off Z^n and preserves the finite strict cap-mass gaps by nonvertical cap continuity. A further sufficiently small common expansion produces a full-dimensional bounded polytope near that point and still avoiding the mixed lattice. The nonempty-Q0 case uses the same bounded threshold expansion and compact-set distance from the closed mixed lattice. Positive spanning prevents an unbounded escape in either limiting argument.

## 2. An exact finite preserving-extension test

Let d>=1. Let P be finite and complete in B=conv(P), and let positive full-dimensional compatible fibers K_p subset R^d define the canonical body C=conv union_p({p} times K_p). Fix q outside B. For each p in P define the finite representation polytope

    R_p(q)={alpha>=0: alpha_q+sum_z alpha_z=1,
                         alpha_q q+sum_z alpha_z z=p}.

For each vertex alpha of R_p(q) with alpha_q>0 impose

    alpha_q x + sum_z alpha_z K_z subset K_p.             (1)

Let E_C(q) be the intersection of these constraints in the unknown continuous point x. It is a closed convex set, possibly empty. There are finitely many representation vertices. If every K_p is polytopal, (1) is a finite list of linear inequalities: for each facet normal u of K_p,

    alpha_q u·x <= h_{K_p}(u)-sum_z alpha_z h_{K_z}(u).    (2)

Then conv(C,(q,x)) preserves every original fiber EXACTLY iff x belongs to E_C(q). Indeed every point of its p-fiber has a representation alpha in R_p(q), and conversely each corresponding Minkowski sum occurs in that fiber. Support functions are linear in alpha. Thus checking its vertices suffices for all representations; alpha_q=0 is already handled by original compatibility. This is an exact finite geometric test, not a volume-only sufficient condition.

Moreover adding this point changes no mixed volume outside P iff

    conv(P union{q}) intersect Z^n = P union{q}.          (3)

The q-fiber is a point because q is an exposed vertex of the enlarged base hull. Any additional new integer base r!=q has a representation r=lambda q+(1-lambda)b with b in B and lambda<1. Its fiber contains a positive homothetic copy of the positive real fiber C_b, so has positive d-volume. Conversely, if (3) holds and x belongs to E_C(q), there are no other integer fibers and the only new one is the zero-volume point at q.

The lemma applies to single-point births. Simultaneous multi-point extensions can have different representation constraints and must be checked jointly.

## 3. A global certificate with no possible preserving integer extension

At bases0,1,2,3 take centered intervals of lengths

    (a,b,b,a),       0<a,       b>2a.                    (4)

Their upper roof is concave and lower roof convex, so these are actual complete positive fibers. Their exact mixed maximum is

    Q=b/2+a,     M=2b+2a,
    beta=1/4+a/[4(a+b)].                               (5)

For completeness, at source(1,0) the upward cap through the source has its only nonnegative slope knots at a/4,a/2,b/2. The masses there are b+a/2,b+a/2,b/2+a; the far positive tail has the last value. Centering gives F(-t)=M-F(t). Hence both cap orientations have minimumQ. The reflected source(2,0) is identical. Large-tilt opposite cap pairs at sources1,2 cover respectively all planes z<=1 and z>=2 and have massQ, proving the global upper bound and including the endpoint candidate fibers.

No convex extension preserving the original fibers can contain ANY point(q,x) at a new integer base. If q=-k<=-1, convexity between (q,x) and the entire length-b fiber at1 forces the fiber at0 to contain an interval of length

    kb/(k+1) >= b/2 > a.

This contradicts preservation of K0, independently of x. The reflected argument excludes every q>=4. This excludes arbitrary extending convex bodies, not only a proposed canonical hull or a chosen point height. More quantitatively, a real extension to base-r<0 requires r<=a/(b-a), and similarly on the right; for b>2a this projection reserve is strictly less than one integer step.

Now retain the genuinely global depth-region certificate explicitly. Take a=1,b=10, so Q=6,M=22. Let the four OPEN caps be

    ±x-6(z-1)>-1/4,       ±x+6(z-2)>-1/4.             (6)

Each has mass25/4. Their closed complements intersect in the full-dimensional diamond

    |x|<=6(z-1)-1/4,
    |x|<=6(2-z)-1/4,

whose projection is[25/24,47/24], disjoint from Z. Each projection facet is the average of its two listed cap inequalities, with continuous normals+1,-1. Thus its two balanced groups cover EVERY integer plane. The contact points are(25/24,0),(47/24,0), and the cap budgets are equal.

Set T=13/2. All cap masses25/4 are strictly belowT. The exact depth region D_T is nonempty: central symmetry about(3/2,0) gives raw depthM/2=11 there. It has no mixed-integer point by (5). Since each cap in (6) has mass<T, D_T is contained in the closed complementary diamond. This satisfies all the nonempty-region and global-lattice-free hypotheses of `candidate 207a0b33a5d3a235`, while the preserving-extension set is empty at EVERY new integer base.

The examples approach the OC bound1/4 as a/b tends to zero. They never go below it; no inference about a hypothetical below-OC minimum is drawn.

## 4. This obstruction has an actual decreasing contraction

Replace both endpoint intervals in (4) by centered intervals of common length a_t=(1-t)a, retaining the two middle intervals. Compatibility remains true and the exact formula (5) continues to hold, including its point-endpoint limit. Thus

    beta(t)=(b/2+a_t)/[2(b+a_t)],
    d beta/d a_t=b/[4(b+a_t)^2]>0.

It strictly decreases until both endpoint fibers become points, leaving two equal positive adjacent fibers and depth1/4. Every intermediate source and cap is controlled by the exact formula. The global-cover obstruction is therefore not an actual variational-minimum counterexample: it shows precisely that global cap coverage does not itself produce a geometric preserving birth.

# Global cap covers and preserving zero-fiber extension

**Finite exact test for preserving point extensions**

Let d>=1, let finite P satisfy conv(P) intersect Z^n=P, and let positive full-dimensional compatible fibers K_p define the canonical hull C=conv(union_p {p} times K_p). Fix q in Z^n outside conv(P). For each p, consider the finite representation polytope of nonnegative coefficients satisfying alpha_q+sum_z alpha_z=1 and alpha_q q+sum_z alpha_z z=p. Then conv(C,(q,x)) preserves every old fiber exactly if and only if, at every vertex with alpha_q>0, alpha_q x+sum_z alpha_z K_z is contained in K_p. These are finitely many convex containment constraints; they are finitely many scalar linear inequalities when all target K_p are polytopal. For a preserving x, the extension adds only the zero-volume point fiber at q if and only if conv(P union {q}) intersect Z^n=P union {q}; any additional integer base receives positive d-volume.

Scope limits: Single-point extension only; simultaneous births require joint representation constraints. The lattice condition is necessary because any new intermediate base receives a positive homothetic copy of an old real fiber.

**Global cap coverage does not imply preserving integer extension**

Four centered interval fibers of lengths (a,b,b,a), b>2a>0, admit a global two-group cap cover but no extension preserving the old fibers can contain any point over a new integer base. Their exact depth is (b/2+a)/(2b+2a). The source gives an explicit globally lattice-free auxiliary diamond for a=1,b=10.

Scope limits: The depth is above 1/4 and decreases to 1/4 under simultaneous endpoint contraction. This is not an obstruction at a hypothetical below-OC minimum.
